tips.title: Leave every construction arc on the page
tips.body: The marks are for the **arcs**, not for the finished line. A perfect perpendicular bisector with the compass marks rubbed out scores almost nothing, because nothing shows it was constructed rather than guessed. Draw them lightly and leave them.

tips.title: Two points give a bisector, two lines give an angle bisector
tips.body: Equidistant from two **points** is the perpendicular bisector of the line joining them. Equidistant from two **lines** is the bisector of the angle between them. Reading which of the two a question means is most of the work.

tips.title: A distance from a line is a racetrack, not a rectangle
tips.body: The locus of points a fixed distance from a line **segment** is two parallel lines alongside it, joined by a **semicircle** at each end. Square corners are the usual mistake: beyond the end of the segment, the nearest point is the endpoint, so the boundary curves round it.

tips.title: Test your shading with one point
tips.body: Once a region is shaded, pick a point well inside it and check it against **every** condition in the question. Then pick one just outside and check that it fails at least one. Ten seconds, and it catches a region shaded on the wrong side.

why.matters:
A locus is the answer to "where could it be?", turned into something you can draw. Each condition in a question — within 5 m of the gate, nearer this wall than that one — is a boundary, and the answer is the region where all of them overlap.

The constructions matter for a separate reason: compasses give an **exact** right angle or an exact half of an angle, with nothing measured. That is why the marks are for the arcs. A bisector drawn by measuring is a guess that happens to be close, and the arcs are the evidence that it was not.

examples.title: How a phone is found from three masts
examples.body:
A mast can tell how far away a phone is without having any idea of the direction. One distance therefore puts the phone somewhere on a **circle** — a locus, exactly as the topic defines it.

Two masts narrow that to where their circles cross, which is two points, not one. In the picture, masts A and B are both 5 km from the phone, and their circles meet at $(5, 4)$ and at $(5, -2)$ — the second is as good an answer as the first on that evidence alone. The third mast, 4 km away, passes through one and not the other, and the ambiguity is gone.

That is why three is the number. GPS does the same thing with spheres instead of circles, and needs one satellite more for the same reason.

visual.alt: Three circles centred on three masts, two of radius five kilometres and one of four, all passing through a single point marked as the phone, with the two larger circles also crossing at a second point lower down that the third circle rules out

examples.title: Why the lanes on a running track start apart
examples.body:
Runners in a one-lap race begin at staggered positions, and the stagger is a locus calculation. A lane's inside edge is the set of points a fixed distance from the line down the middle of the field — two straights with a **semicircle** at each end, the racetrack shape rather than a rectangle.

The straights are the same length in every lane, so the whole difference is in the bends. Two semicircles make one circle, and a lane one width further out has a radius bigger by that width. A circle's circumference is $2\pi r$, so the extra is $2\pi \times 1.22 = 7.7$ m a lane, whatever the radius happens to be.

Over eight lanes that is 54 m, which is why lane 8 starts most of a straight ahead of lane 1. The stagger is not a handicap; it is the amount that makes the lap lengths equal.

props.title: A lap, if every lane started level

visual.alt: A table of eight running lanes showing that each one further out adds about seven point seven metres to the lap, so lane eight would run four hundred and fifty three point seven metres against lane one's four hundred

examples.title: Which recycling centre you are sent to
examples.body:
A council with two tips sends each household to the nearer one, and the boundary between the two areas on the map is a **perpendicular bisector**. Every point on it is the same distance from both, which is the definition the construction is built to produce.

With tips at $(3.5, 8)$ and $(6.5, 2)$, the line joining them has gradient $-2$, so the bisector has gradient $0.5$ and passes through the midpoint $(5, 5)$: $y = 0.5x + 2.5$. A house at $(2, 6)$ sits above that line, and checking it directly agrees — $2.50$ km to the first tip against $6.02$ to the second.

Add a third tip and you get another two bisectors and a three-way junction where they meet. Carry on and the map fills with straight-sided cells, one per tip. The same picture decides mobile phone cells, school catchments and which shop's delivery van comes to your door.

visual.alt: Two recycling tips plotted with the perpendicular bisector of the line joining them drawn right across the map, and a house marked on the upper left side of it, nearer the first tip

steps.title: What a construction is, and why the arcs matter
steps.body:
A **construction** is an accurate drawing made with a **ruler and compasses only** — no protractor, and no measuring of angles.

> The marks are for the **arcs**, not for the finished line.

That is the single most important thing about this topic. A perpendicular bisector drawn perfectly by eye, with the compass marks rubbed out, scores almost nothing: there is nothing on the page to show it was constructed rather than guessed. Draw the arcs lightly and **leave them**.

Four standard constructions are needed, and three of them are the same idea.

**The perpendicular bisector of a line $AB$.** Open the compasses to more than half of $AB$. With the point on $A$, draw arcs above and below the line. Without changing the radius, do the same from $B$. The arcs cross at two points; join them. That line cuts $AB$ in half, at right angles.

**The bisector of an angle.** Put the compass point on the vertex and draw an arc crossing both arms. From each of those two crossings, draw an arc in the middle. Join the vertex to where they meet.

**A perpendicular from a point to a line.** From the point, draw an arc crossing the line twice. From those two crossings, draw arcs that meet. Join the point to where they meet.

**A perpendicular at a point on a line.** Draw a short arc either side of the point, along the line, then treat those two marks as $A$ and $B$ and build a perpendicular bisector.

Notice that all four come down to the same move: two arcs of equal radius, crossing.

steps.body: The compass radius is set once at the start of each and then left alone. Changing it partway is what makes a construction come out crooked.

steps.note: do not change the radius after this

steps.text: Point on $B$: draw two more arcs, crossing the first pair

steps.note: which is what makes it a locus as well as a construction

check.prompt: When constructing a perpendicular bisector of $AB$, how wide must the compasses be opened?
check.solution: The arcs from $A$ and from $B$ have to overlap. If the radius is less than half of $AB$ they never reach each other, and if it is exactly half they touch at a single point on the line itself, which gives nothing to join.

steps.title: The four basic loci
steps.body:
A **locus** is the set of all points obeying a rule. There are four to know, and a question is usually one of them in disguise.

**1. A fixed distance from a point** is a **circle**, with that point as centre and that distance as radius. "Within" that distance means the circle **and everything inside it**.

**2. Equidistant from two points** is the **perpendicular bisector** of the line joining them. Every point on it is the same distance from both.

**3. Equidistant from two lines** is the **bisector of the angle** between them.

**4. A fixed distance from a line segment** is a **racetrack**: two parallel lines running alongside it, joined by a **semicircle** at each end.

> That fourth one is the one people get wrong. It is not a rectangle.

The reason is worth understanding. Alongside the segment, the nearest point of it is directly across, so the boundary runs parallel. But **past the end**, the nearest point is the **endpoint itself** — and everywhere a fixed distance from a single point is part of a circle. So the boundary curves round each end.

**Reading the words matters.**

- "Equidistant from $A$ and $B$" is the bisector itself, a line.
- "Nearer to $A$ than to $B$" is everything on $A$'s **side** of that bisector, a region.
- "Within $5$ m of $P$" is the disc, boundary included.
- "More than $5$ m from $P$" is everything outside it.

steps.title: Regions from several conditions
steps.body:
Most exam questions give **two or three** conditions at once and ask for the region satisfying all of them.

**The method.**

1. Take each condition on its own and draw its boundary.
2. Decide which side of each boundary satisfies that condition.
3. Shade only where **every** condition holds — the overlap.

> Shade the overlap, not the union. A point has to pass **all** the tests.

**Read the scale before setting the compasses.** A plan at $1$ cm to $2$ m needs a $5$ m radius drawn as $2.5$ cm. Applying the scale at the end, after drawing, does not work.

**Boundaries: solid or dashed?**

- "Within $5$ m" and "at least $5$ m" **include** the boundary, so draw it solid.
- "Less than $5$ m" and "nearer to $A$ than $B$" **exclude** it, so draw it dashed.

Say which you have used; a sentence costs nothing and removes any doubt.

**Then test it.** Take a point well inside your shaded region and check it against every condition in the question, then take one just outside and check that it fails at least one. This catches shading on the wrong side of a bisector, which is the most common error, and it takes ten seconds.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
**Part A — name the locus.**

1. All points exactly $4$ m from a point $P$.
2. All points equidistant from two points $A$ and $B$.
3. All points equidistant from two walls that meet at a corner.
4. All points exactly $2$ m from a straight wall of finite length.

**Part B — construct.**

6. Draw any angle and construct its bisector. Leave your arcs.

**Part C — regions.**

7. A goat is tied to a post $P$ by a $3$ m rope, in a field whose north fence is $2$ m from the post. Describe and sketch the region the goat can reach.
8. Two trees stand at $A(1, 1)$ and $B(7, 1)$. Shade the region that is nearer to $A$ than to $B$ **and** within $4$ m of $A$. Say whether each boundary is solid or dashed.

For question 8, draw both boundaries before shading anything.

steps.title: Going deeper: scale, three conditions, and testing the answer
steps.body:
**Scale is applied when you set the compasses, not afterwards.** A plan is drawn at $1$ cm to $2$ m and a question asks for points within $5$ m of a post. The compass radius is

$$5 \div 2 = 2.5 \text{ cm}.$$

Drawing a $5$ cm circle and mentioning the scale in a sentence underneath does not recover the mark. Work the radius out first, write it down, then set the compasses.

**Three conditions at once.** Take them one at a time.

A treasure lies within $6$ m of the oak at $A$, nearer to the oak than to the elm at $B$, and at least $2$ m from the wall. Draw:

1. a circle of radius $6$ about $A$ — shade inside;
2. the perpendicular bisector of $AB$ — keep $A$'s side;
3. the racetrack boundary $2$ m from the wall — keep **outside** it.

Then shade only where all three overlap. Each boundary is drawn on its own before any shading happens, because trying to shade as you go makes the overlap impossible to see.

**Deciding which side.** Do not reason it out — **test a point**. Pick somewhere obviously on one side, work out whether it satisfies the condition, and shade that side if it does. It is faster than thinking and it does not go wrong.

**Then check the finished region.** One point well inside must pass **every** condition; one point just outside must fail **at least one**. If your inside point fails something, you have shaded on the wrong side of one boundary — and this check finds which.

**Why the end of a wall curves, once more.** At a point beyond the end of the wall, the closest part of the wall is the endpoint. Everywhere a fixed distance from a single point lies on a circle centred there. So the boundary must be circular round each end, and a rectangle would wrongly include the corners, which are further away than the stated distance.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- A **construction** uses ruler and compasses only, never a protractor.
- **Leave every arc on the page.** The arcs are the method, and the method is the marks.
- Do not change the compass radius partway through a construction.
- **Perpendicular bisector**: equal arcs from each end, opened to more than half the line.
- **Angle bisector**: an arc across both arms, then equal arcs from those two crossings.
- **A fixed distance from a point** is a **circle**.
- **Equidistant from two points** is the **perpendicular bisector** of the line joining them.
- **Equidistant from two lines** is the **angle bisector**.
- **A fixed distance from a line segment** is a **racetrack**: two parallels with a **semicircle at each end**, never a rectangle.
- "Equidistant" gives a **line**; "nearer to" gives a **region**.
- Apply the **scale** when you set the compasses, not afterwards.
- "Within" and "at least" include the boundary — solid. "Less than" and "nearer to" exclude it — dashed.
- Draw **every** boundary first, then shade the **overlap**.
- **Test the shading**: one point inside must pass every condition, one just outside must fail one.

questions.prompt:
A rectangular garden is drawn to a scale of $1$ cm to $2$ m. A post $P$ stands in the garden, and a straight wall runs along one side.

(a) A goat is tied to $P$ by a rope $6$ m long. State the locus of points it can reach, and the compass radius you would use on the plan.

(b) A path is to be laid so that it is always $4$ m from the wall. Describe the shape of this locus, explaining what happens at each end of the wall.

(c) Explain how you would shade the region that is both within $6$ m of $P$ and more than $4$ m from the wall.
questions.skill: shading a region from several conditions
questions.solution: For part a, the goat can reach any point whose distance from the post is six metres or less, so the locus of the furthest points it can reach is a circle of radius six metres centred on P, and the region it can reach is that circle together with everything inside it. On the plan the scale is one centimetre to two metres, so the radius must be divided by two: six divided by two is three, so I would set the compasses to three centimetres. The scale is applied at the moment the compasses are set, not afterwards. For part b, alongside the wall the nearest point of the wall to any position is directly across from it, so the path runs parallel to the wall, four metres away, on each side. At each end of the wall the situation changes: past the end there is no more wall, so the nearest part of it is the endpoint itself. Everywhere exactly four metres from a single point lies on a circle centred there, so the path curves round each end in a semicircular arc of radius four metres. The whole locus is therefore a racetrack shape, not a rectangle; drawing square corners would put points in the path that are more than four metres from the wall. For part c, draw both boundaries first, before shading anything. Draw the circle of radius three centimetres about P for the first condition, and the racetrack boundary four metres from the wall for the second. Then decide which side of each is wanted: inside the circle, because the goat must be within six metres, and outside the racetrack, because the region must be more than four metres from the wall. Shade only where those two overlap. Finally, test it: pick a point well inside the shading and check it is both within six metres of P and more than four metres from the wall, then pick one just outside and check it fails one of those.

On the plan the scale is one centimetre to two metres, so the radius must be divided by two: six divided by two is three, so I would set the compasses to three centimetres. The scale is applied at the moment the compasses are set, not afterwards. For part b, alongside the wall the nearest point of the wall to any position is directly across from it, so the path runs parallel to the wall, four metres away, on each side. At each end of the wall the situation changes: past the end there is no more wall, so the nearest part of it is the endpoint itself. Everywhere exactly four metres from a single point lies on a circle centred there, so the path curves round each end in a semicircular arc of radius four metres. The whole locus is therefore a racetrack shape, not a rectangle; drawing square corners would put points in the path that are more than four metres from the wall. For part c, draw both boundaries first, before shading anything. Draw the circle of radius three centimetres about P for the first condition, and the racetrack boundary four metres from the wall for the second. Then decide which side of each is wanted: inside the circle, because the goat must be within six metres, and outside the racetrack, because the region must be more than four metres from the wall. Shade only where those two overlap. Finally, test it: pick a point well inside the shading and check it is both within six metres of P and more than four metres from the wall, then pick one just outside and check it fails one of those.

questions.prompt:
Two trees stand at $A(1, 1)$ and $B(7, 1)$ on a grid marked in metres.

(a) Find the equation of the locus of points equidistant from $A$ and $B$, and show that the point $(4, 5)$ lies on it.

(b) Describe, and say how you would draw, the region that is nearer to $A$ than to $B$ **and** within $4$ m of $A$.

(c) State whether each boundary of that region should be solid or dashed, with a reason.
questions.solution: For part a, the locus of points equidistant from two fixed points is the perpendicular bisector of the line joining them. A is at one comma one and B is at seven comma one, so the line AB is horizontal and its midpoint is at four comma one. The perpendicular bisector is therefore the vertical line through that midpoint, which has equation x equals four. To show that four comma five lies on it, work out both distances. From A at one comma one to four comma five, the differences are three across and four up, so by Pythagoras the distance is the square root of nine plus sixteen, which is the square root of twenty five, which is five metres. From B at seven comma one to four comma five, the differences are three across the other way and four up, so the distance is again the square root of nine plus sixteen, which is five metres. The two distances are equal, so the point lies on the locus. For part b, the region has two conditions. Nearer to A than to B means everything on A's side of the line x equals four, which is the region where x is less than four. Within four metres of A means inside a circle of radius four centred on one comma one. To draw it, put in the circle first, then the vertical line x equals four, and then shade only the part of the circle that lies to the left of that line, since a point must satisfy both conditions. For part c, the circle should be solid, because within four metres includes points exactly four metres away, so the boundary is part of the region. The line x equals four should be dashed, because nearer to A than to B excludes points that are exactly the same distance from both, and every point on that line is equidistant. Saying which convention has been used removes any doubt about whether the edges count.

examTechnique.body:
**Use compasses, and do not change the radius mid-construction.** Most of these constructions depend on two arcs of the same radius. Setting the compass once and leaving it is what makes them work.

**Leave the arcs showing.** They are the evidence, and the method marks are for them.

**Translate the words into a locus before drawing anything.**

| The question says | The locus is |
| --- | --- |
| within $5$ m of a point | a circle of radius $5$, and the inside of it |
| equidistant from two points | the perpendicular bisector of the line joining them |
| equidistant from two lines | the bisector of the angle between them |
| within $3$ m of a wall | a pair of parallel lines with a semicircle at each end |
| nearer to $A$ than to $B$ | one side of the perpendicular bisector of $AB$ |

**Read the scale first.** A plan drawn at $1$ cm to $2$ m needs the compass set to $2.5$ cm for a distance of $5$ m. Setting it to $5$ cm is a very easy mark to lose.

**"Within" includes the boundary; "nearer to" does not.** A solid line means the boundary counts, a dashed one that it does not — say which you have used.

**Shade only where every condition is satisfied**, not where any one of them is. Draw each boundary first, then shade the overlap.
examinerErrors: Rubbing out the construction arcs, leaving no evidence of the method.
Changing the compass radius partway through a bisector.
Drawing a rectangle for "within 3 m of a wall" instead of rounding the ends.
Bisecting the angle when the question asked for points equidistant from two **points**.
Forgetting the scale, so a 5 m radius is drawn as 5 cm on a 1 cm to 2 m plan.
Shading where one condition holds rather than where all of them hold.
Shading the wrong side of a perpendicular bisector, so the region is nearer the wrong point.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer reads each phrase in the question and names the locus it describes before touching the compasses. It applies the scale at the moment it sets the radius, rather than at the end. It leaves every arc on the page, because the arcs are the method. It rounds the ends of a distance-from-a-line region instead of drawing a rectangle, knowing that beyond the end of a segment the nearest point is the endpoint. It shades only the overlap of all the conditions, and then tests the shading by taking one point inside and one just outside and checking each against every condition in turn.
